article_title: Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Tactical game-centered approaches as a family of game-centered pedagogies grounded in constructivist and situated learning
description: TGAs are a family of PE teaching approaches, originating with the Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) model proposed in 1982, in which structured, modified small-sided games are the central context through which learners develop tactical, technical and strategic skills. The review states the variants "share common elements related to cognitive, constructivist, and situated learning theories", with learners generating their own solutions through problem-solving and responding to teacher questioning. Variants named include play practice, tactical games approach, tactical-decision learning model, and game sense. The review situates TGAs within an ecological dynamics, constraints-led perspective of skill acquisition.
requirements: A TGA unit of at least four consecutive lessons, per the review's eligibility criteria
Modified games with manipulated task constraints (rules, aims, scoring, playing area, number of players) creating tactical problems
constraints: The review notes there is only a little evidence showing transfer of knowledge and skills across different games within a category
TGAs are suggested as more suitable from upper primary school years, aged 9 onwards
target_learners: Primary and secondary school physical education students
target_learning_goals: Technical skill development through game contexts
examples: Included interventions used terminology TGfU (n = 11), TGA (n = 6), tactical games model (n = 4), and game-centered approach (n = 3)
key_sources: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236

article_title: The Application of the Teaching Games for Understanding in Physical Education. Systematic Review of the Last Six Years.
citation: Barba-Martín Raúl A., Bores-García Daniel, Hortigüela-Alcalá David, González-Calvo Gustavo. (2020). The Application of the Teaching Games for Understanding in Physical Education. Systematic Review of the Last Six Years. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17093330
title: Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) model: game-centered sports teaching built on four pedagogical principles
description: TGfU emerged in the 1980s as an alternative to the technical method for teaching sports games, making understanding of sport the focus of learning and asking students to consider the "why" of doing something during the development of the game, rather than the "how". It develops tactics and skills in real or simulated game contexts to improve decision-making and problem-solving, with the teacher questioning students to build tactical awareness. The review describes it as resting on four pedagogical principles: transfer, modification-representation, modification-exaggeration and tactical complexity.
requirements: Implementation requires teachers to have thorough knowledge of the model itself and of each discipline to make appropriate modifications during development
constraints: The review notes misinterpretations of the model have occurred, leading the original creators to publish clarifications
target_learners: primary and secondary school Physical Education students
target_learning_goals: tactical awareness and decision-making in games
cognitive, affective, social and physical learning in sport
key_sources: Barba-Martín Raúl A., Bores-García Daniel, Hortigüela-Alcalá David, González-Calvo Gustavo. (2020). The Application of the Teaching Games for Understanding in Physical Education. Systematic Review of the Last Six Years. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17093330

title: TGfU game classification into four categories supporting transfer between similar sports
description: To establish common guidelines among sports, TGfU developed classifications grouping games mainly into four categories: target games, court or net/wall games, striking/fielding games, and territory or invasion games. The review explains that this lets "teachers help students to compare more easily the similarities of apparently different games", for example extrapolating between basketball and football as invasion games. This classification underpins the model's transfer principle.
requirements: Games must be grouped by structural similarities so tactical aspects common to different sports can be transferred
target_learners: primary and secondary school Physical Education students

article_title: Using Cooperative Teams-Game-Tournament in 11 Religious School to Improve Mathematics Understanding and Communication
citation: Veloo, A., Md-Ali, R., & Chairany, S. (2016). Using Cooperative Teams-Game-Tournament in 11 Religious School to Improve Mathematics Understanding and Communication. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 13(2), 97-123. http://mjli.uum.edu.my
title: Teams-Games-Tournament: a cooperative learning structure of teams, games and tournament
description: Teams-Games-Tournament (TGT), developed by Edwards and De Vries (1972) and elaborated by Slavin, is a cooperative learning approach combining learning groups with team tournaments. The article describes it as involving "cooperation among students in small groups, whereby students are encouraged to help each other to accomplish a given task." It has three basic elements: teams (students randomly assigned to stable teams of similar abilities), games (teacher-designed exercises), and tournament (students represent their teams and compete individually against students of the same ability level from other teams, with individual scores contributing to team scores).
requirements: Heterogeneous learning groups of four to five students in terms of ability, gender and race
Tournament competitors matched at the same ability level
Worksheets as the primary instructional materials
constraints: During the tournament each member plays individually without help from other team members
target_learners: Grade 11 secondary students in religious schools
examples: In the study, the experimental group experienced five weeks of cooperative TGT with teams, games and tournaments before post-test 1, after which TGT was withdrawn for five weeks before post-test 2.
key_sources: Veloo, A., Md-Ali, R., & Chairany, S. (2016). Using Cooperative Teams-Game-Tournament in 11 Religious School to Improve Mathematics Understanding and Communication. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 13(2), 97-123. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1134733

article_title: The Effect of Dynamic Geometry Software and Physical Manipulatives on Candidate Teachers' Transformational Geometry Success
citation: Gül Kaleli Yılmaz. (2015). The Effect of Dynamic Geometry Software and Physical Manipulatives on Candidate Teachers’ Transformational Geometry Success. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.5.2610
title: Transformational Geometry Achievement Test (TGAT): 30 questions across recognition, features, and construction sections
description: The TGAT is a 30-question achievement test developed for this study, with 10 questions per dimension covering recognition (identifying which transformation is applied), features (matching features to transformations), and construction (performing transformations on shapes). Questions were drawn from an item pool, reviewed by specialist academicians including a Turkish language specialist, and scored 1 point per correct answer for a 0–30 total.
requirements: Items were vetted by a specialist academician and checked for comprehensibility and readability by a Turkish language specialist before finalization.
constraints: The article notes prior studies used routine achievement tests that did not focus on separate sections; this test was designed to distinguish defining, stating features, and forming transformations.
target_learning_goals: transformational geometry achievement across recognition, features, and construction
examples: Recognition items showed ten mixed shapes and asked which transformation was applied; construction items asked students to perform transformations such as reflection according to a line or a two-unit displacement to the right.
key_sources: Gül Kaleli Yılmaz. (2015). The Effect of Dynamic Geometry Software and Physical Manipulatives on Candidate Teachers’ Transformational Geometry Success. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.5.2610

article_title: The Effect of Cooperative Learning Model of Teams Games Tournament (TGT) and Students' Motivation toward Physics Learning Outcome
citation: Nadrah, Ismail Tolla, Muhammad Sidin Ali & Muris. (2017). The Effect of Cooperative Learning Model of Teams Games Tournament (TGT) and Students' Motivation toward Physics Learning Outcome. International Education Studies, 10(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n2p123
title: Teams Games Tournament five-stage structure
description: The TGT cooperative learning model proceeds through five stages the article enumerates: "The first stage is class presentation. The second stage is learning in groups or teams. The third stage is playing games. The fourth stage is a tournament... The fifth stage is teams' recognition." Students act as peer tutors and compete for group points, with recognition tiers based on group average scores.
requirements: Students must be organised into teams and compete in tournaments according to ability level
target_learners: senior high school students (class X) studying physics
examples: Class X3 at SMAN 2 Makassar was treated with TGT while class X9 received traditional learning
key_sources: Nadrah, Ismail Tolla, Muhammad Sidin Ali & Muris. (2017). The Effect of Cooperative Learning Model of Teams Games Tournament (TGT) and Students' Motivation toward Physics Learning Outcome. International Education Studies, 10(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n2p123
